_about: Choice-only grading regression fixture (2026-09-28). Harmful/measured/off-topic/maxwell cases and taps come from the Phase 1 offline replay of 457 scripted physics lessons on production; real = 65 anonymised human-cadence replies to a served quiz (internal accounts). No names, emails or ids.

quizzes.q: A road is 3 kilometres long. How many metres is that? (1 km = 1000 m)
o: 3000 m — because a metre is smaller than a kilometre, so more of them are needed
3 m or 0.003 m — dividing instead of multiplying by 1000

quizzes.q: To raise a satellite into a HIGHER circular orbit you fire the engine and speed it up. Once it has settled into the new orbit, is it moving faster or slower than before?
o: It depends on the mass of the satellite
At exactly the same speed, in a bigger circle
Slower — orbital speed falls as √(GM/r), so a higher orbit is a slower one. The energy went into gravitational potential
Faster — you fired the engine, so it must be going faster

quizzes.q: Why does a small droplet of water in free fall take up a spherical shape?
o: Water molecules repel one another and spread out as evenly as they can
A sphere has the smallest surface area for a given volume, and surface tension acts to minimise surface area
Gravity acts equally in all directions on a falling object
The surrounding air pushes on it equally from every direction

quizzes.q: You pass an already-isolated beam of red light (separated from white light by an earlier prism) through a SECOND prism. What happens?
o: The second prism creates additional new colors from the red light, the same way the first prism apparently created colors from white light
Only red comes out, further deflected but not split into new colors — the first prism never "created" colors, it only separated frequencies already present in the original white light

quizzes.q: You add heat steadily to a mixture of ice and water at 1 atm, while some ice still remains unmelted. What happens to the temperature reading?
o: It continues rising steadily throughout, since heat is continuously being added to the mixture
It stays EXACTLY FIXED at 0°C for as long as any ice remains — all the added heat goes into breaking intermolecular bonds (melting), not into raising temperature, until all the ice is gone

quizzes.q: In a SERIES circuit, which quantity is the same at every point?
o: The power dissipated in each component
The current
The potential difference across each component
The resistance of each component

quizzes.q: You move ten times further away. By what factor does a POINT CHARGE's field fall, and by what factor does a DIPOLE's?
o: Both by 1/100 — every electrostatic field obeys the inverse square law
Point charge by 1/100 (inverse square), dipole by 1/1000 (inverse cube) — the dipole's two opposite charges nearly cancel at a distance, so its field dies away faster

quizzes.q: A single proton sits alone in an otherwise empty vacuum chamber. Is there an electric field 1 cm away from it?
o: Yes — E = kq/r^2 is fixed by the source charge alone. A test charge is how we would MEASURE the field, not what brings it into existence
No — with nothing at that point to feel a force, there is no field there

quizzes.q: You want the field around a very long uniformly charged wire. Can Gauss's law be used, given a wire is not a sphere?
o: No — Gauss's law applies only to spherically symmetric charge distributions
Yes — use a coaxial CYLINDRICAL Gaussian surface. Gauss's law holds for every closed surface; the symmetry only decides whether the flux integral is easy, and a long wire has cylindrical symmetry

quizzes.q: At the exact moment the current in an LC circuit reaches its maximum value I_max, how is the total energy split between the capacitor and the inductor?
o: Roughly 50% in each, since both components are actively involved when current is flowing
0% in the capacitor, 100% in the inductor — at maximum current, the charge Q is exactly zero, so the capacitor holds no energy at all

quizzes.q: Two loops sit in the same uniform 0.5 T field. Loop A has area 0.02 m^2 facing the field; loop B has the same area but is turned edge-on. Compare their fluxes.
o: Equal — both sit in the same 0.5 T field, and the flux is the field strength
0.01 Wb through A and zero through B — flux is B*A*cos(theta), so orientation and area matter as much as the field. Same field, different flux

quizzes.q: You hold the current and the TOTAL number of turns fixed, then stretch a solenoid to twice its length AND double its radius. What happens to the internal field?
o: It roughly doubles — the solenoid is much wider now, and a wider solenoid produces a stronger field inside
It halves — B = mu_0 * n * I depends on turns per unit LENGTH, so doubling the length halves n. The radius does not appear in B at all; it changes the inductance and the flux, not the field strength
Nothing changes — the field is set by the total number of turns and the current, and neither changed

quizzes.q: Force A = 800 N for 0.002 s; Force B = 8 N for 0.2 s. Which delivers more impulse?
o: Equal — J_A = 1.6 N·s = J_B = 1.6 N·s
A, because it is a much bigger force

quizzes.q: A motor delivers a steady 1500 W. How much work does it do in 20 s?
o: 1500 J — the power is the work
75 J — dividing the power by the time

quizzes.q: A free particle moving in 1D has L=½mẋ². Does it have a Noether symmetry leading to a conserved quantity?
o: No — Noether symmetries require the system to look geometrically symmetric (spherical or cylindrical), and a point particle has no such shape
Yes — L is independent of x (∂L/∂x=0), a genuine translational symmetry, so p_x is conserved by Noether's theorem, regardless of the absence of visible shape

quizzes.q: Of these three — (i) heat flows hot→cold, (ii) gas expands into vacuum, (iii) two gases unmix spontaneously — which violates the second law?
o: Only (iii) — spontaneous unmixing decreases entropy with no external work
All three violate it, since entropy always increases

quizzes.q: On a force–time graph for a collision, what does the AREA under the curve represent, and why does that matter?
o: The impulse, and therefore the change in momentum — which is what makes a violently varying collision force usable, since only the area matters
The momentum of the object, rather than its change
The average force during the collision
The work done during the collision

quizzes.q: For a central-force problem, {L_z,H}=0. What does this bracket vanishing actually mean?
o: L_z is conserved under the Hamiltonian flow generated by H — the bracket vanishing is a statement about dynamics (L_z does not change over time), not about L_z and H being unrelated
L_z and H are independent, unrelated functions that do not interact with each other

quizzes.q: At 0 K a perfect crystal has exactly one possible arrangement (Ω = 1), while a glass is frozen into an enormous number of arrangements. What are their entropies at 0 K?
o: Both are large — all motion stops, so disorder is maximal
Both are exactly 0 — the Third Law says entropy is zero at absolute zero
Crystal S = 0; glass keeps a large RESIDUAL entropy, because S = k_B lnΩ and its Ω is huge

quizzes.q: In empty space far from any charges or currents, can Faraday's law and the Ampere-Maxwell law be applied completely independently of each other?
o: Yes — each of Maxwell's four equations is a self-contained, independent rule that can be applied and solved on its own

No — they form a coupled feedback loop: a changing B (via Faraday) creates a circulating E, which (via Ampere-Maxwell) creates a circulating B, and solving BOTH together produces the electromagnetic wave equation

quizzes.q: A desk edge measures 1.5 metres, and the exact same edge measures about 5 feet. Do metres and feet represent different dimensions?
o: Yes — different units mean different dimensions, since the numbers 1.5 and 5 are completely different
No — both are simply different UNITS (scales) for measuring the same dimension, length [L]; the underlying kind of quantity never changes when you switch units

quizzes.q: A student writes an equation that includes the term "3 metres + 5 seconds." Is this a physically meaningful expression?
o: Yes — as long as the numbers work out arithmetically, the terms can be added regardless of what they represent
No — only quantities of the SAME dimension can be added; length and time are different dimensions, and there is no physical quantity that "3 metres + 5 seconds" could represent

quizzes.q: Three worn rulers all consistently read 12.41 cm on the same object every time, but all three start 2 mm past the true zero mark. Are these readings precise, accurate, both, or neither?
o: Both precise and accurate — since all three rulers agree with each other, the consistent reading must be correct
Precise but NOT accurate — the readings cluster tightly together (precision), but they are all systematically offset from the true value (inaccurate)

quizzes.q: You repeat a measurement many times and take the mean. Which kind of error does that reduce?
o: Both kinds, equally
Neither — averaging changes nothing about the uncertainty
Random error only — systematic error survives averaging completely untouched
Systematic error only

quizzes.q: Two forces, of 3 N and 4 N, act on the same point. What is the SMALLEST magnitude their resultant can have?
o: 0 N — any two forces can be arranged to cancel
5 N — the perpendicular case
1 N — when they point in exactly opposite directions
7 N — the two magnitudes added

quizzes.q: Every physical quantity is essentially a number — you can add temperature, time and force the same way. Is that right, or does something depend on more than a number?
o: No — some quantities need a DIRECTION as well as a magnitude, and they combine differently for it. Two 5 N forces in the SAME direction give a net 10 N; two 5 N forces in OPPOSITE directions give net 0 N; two 5 N forces at right angles give ~7 N at 45°. Same magnitudes, three different physical outcomes — scalars alone (temperature, time, mass) cannot produce that. Force, displacement, velocity, acceleration and momentum are vectors precisely because direction changes the physics
Yes — all physical quantities are just numbers; direction is a description, not a quantity

quizzes.q: Taking east as positive, a hiker's displacement is −2 km. What does this mean?
o: She ended up 2 km west of her start — the sign is the direction
The measurement is invalid — displacement cannot be negative
She walked 2 km less than planned

quizzes.q: How many significant figures in 0.00420? In 4002?
o: 5 in 0.00420 and 4 in 4002, counting every digit shown
3 in 0.00420 (leading zeros don't count, trailing zero after decimal does); 4 in 4002 (embedded zeros count)

quizzes.q: A ruler measures only to the nearest millimetre. A calculator, using that measurement, outputs an area of 7.853975 cm². How many of these digits are actually trustworthy?
o: Only as many as the original millimetre-precision measurement supports — the trailing digits (.853975) are arithmetic noise the ruler never measured
All of them — the calculator computed them precisely, so all the displayed digits are trustworthy and should be reported

quizzes.q: You measured two lengths: 12.3 cm and 0.056 cm. Adding them, what is the result you should report with correct precision?
A 1-metre stick is measured against centimetre marks and spans exactly 100 of them. Does converting from metres (1) to centimetres (100) mean the stick got longer?
o: No — the stick's physical length never changed; only the SIZE of the unit changed, and since a centimetre is a smaller unit, more of them are needed for the same length
The number 100 is bigger than 1, so converting to a bigger unit should always give a bigger number, confirming the stick is effectively "more" in centimetres

quizzes.q: To convert 4000 mm to metres, do you multiply or divide by 1000?
o: Divide — going from a smaller unit (mm) to a bigger unit (m) makes the number smaller
Multiply — converting units always means multiplying by the conversion factor

quizzes.q: You are converting 4 megametres to metres, using the rule "kilo means add three zeros" applied to mega instead. What goes wrong?
o: Mega represents 10⁶ (six zeros), not 10³ (three zeros) like kilo — "add three zeros" only worked for kilo by coincidence and gives the wrong answer (4,000 instead of the correct 4,000,000) for mega
Nothing goes wrong — "add three zeros" is a universal rule that works for any metric prefix

quizzes.q: Which of these is NOT one of the seven SI base units?
o: The second
The ampere
The newton — it is derived, standing for kg·m·s⁻²
The kilogram

quizzes.q: A component is labelled 4.7 µF (microfarads). Written in farads, what is that?
o: 4.7 × 10⁻³ F — micro is the same as milli

quizzes.q: Force has SI units kg·m·s⁻². Reading that dimensionally, what does it tell you force IS?
o: Mass divided by a time, since seconds appear underneath
A base quantity in its own right that happens to be written in other units
Mass multiplied by an acceleration — the units are the definition, written out

quizzes.q: 3 N and 4 N at right angles: is the resultant 7 N or 5 N?
o: 5 N — vectors at an angle combine via the Pythagorean/triangle rule, not simple addition
7 N — magnitudes simply add together regardless of angle

quizzes.q: Two people push equally hard (5 N each) on opposite sides of a box, directly opposing each other. What is the magnitude of the net (resultant) force on the box?
o: 10 N — combining two forces should always produce something bigger than either force alone
0 N — the two equal, oppositely-directed forces cancel completely; combining two nonzero vectors can produce a result smaller than either one, even exactly zero

quizzes.q: A cyclist slows steadily from 8 m/s to 2 m/s over 3 s. What is the acceleration?
o: −2 m/s² — the minus sign says the change opposes the motion
−6 m/s² — the velocity fell by 6
2 m/s² — acceleration is a size, so the sign can be dropped
−0.5 m/s² — 3 s divided by the 6 m/s change

quizzes.q: A key is released from rest. At the exact instant of release, v = 0. What is its acceleration at that instant?
o: Undefined, because you cannot divide by a zero velocity
9.8 m/s² downward — a is the RATE v is changing, which does not depend on the value of v
Zero — it is not moving yet, so nothing is accelerating

quizzes.q: A ball is thrown straight up. At the very top, its velocity is zero. Does it have an acceleration at that moment? Why?
o: No — it isn’t moving at that instant so it can’t be accelerating
Yes — still 9.8 m/s² downward; velocity is zero but is changing at that instant

quizzes.q: A 1 kg steel cube (V=1.28×10⁻⁴ m³) is at 5 m depth, then lowered to 20 m depth. How does the buoyant force change?
o: It stays the same (1.25 N) — buoyant force depends only on displaced volume, not depth
It increases at greater depth, since water pressure is higher

quizzes.q: A block floats in water with exactly one third of its volume above the surface. What is the density of the block? (Water: 1000 kg/m³)
o: About 667 kg/m³
1500 kg/m³
1000 kg/m³ — anything that floats matches the water
About 333 kg/m³ — matching the fraction ABOVE the surface

quizzes.q: A runner goes once around a 400 m circular track and finishes exactly where she started. What is her displacement for the lap?
o: 200 m — half of the lap
0 m — she ends at the same point she started from
It cannot be found without knowing her speed
400 m — the length of the track

quizzes.q: A cat walks 5 m east and then 2 m west. Taking east as positive, what is its displacement?
o: 7 m — the total distance walked
+3 m (3 m east) — 5 m east minus 2 m back
−3 m — it finished by walking west
+2 m — only the last part of the walk counts

quizzes.q: Δx = x_f − x_i = −8 m. What type of quantity is this, and what does the negative sign mean?
o: Displacement — a vector; the negative sign means the net motion is leftward (negative direction)
Distance — negative just means it was measured backward

quizzes.q: Two forces of 10 N act on the same object, one to the left and one to the right. Are they the same force?
o: Yes — both are 10 N, and magnitude is what defines a force
No — force is a vector, so equal magnitudes in opposite directions are different forces; here they sum to zero
Yes, and they therefore add to 20 N

quizzes.q: A crate slides across a floor at a perfectly constant velocity. What does that tell you about the forces on it?
o: The NET force is zero — constant velocity requires no net force, though individual forces (push, friction) are certainly acting
No forces of any kind are acting on it
There must be a net forward force, otherwise it would stop

quizzes.q: Classify as contact or non-contact: gravity on the Moon’s surface.
o: Non-contact — gravity acts at a distance, no touching required
Contact — the Moon is being pulled by something touching it

quizzes.q: A coasting puck slides across frictionless ice at constant speed. Should a forward "motion force" appear on its free-body diagram?
o: Yes — a forward force is needed in the direction of motion to keep it moving
No — only weight (down) and normal force (up) belong on the diagram

quizzes.q: A puck slides across frictionless ice at constant velocity, with nothing touching it. Which horizontal force belongs on its free-body diagram?
o: A forward "force of motion" in the direction it is sliding
None — the horizontal diagram is empty; the puck coasts by inertia

quizzes.q: A 10 kg crate slides across a level floor with a coefficient of kinetic friction of 0.3. What is the friction force on it? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
o: 3 N — μ times the mass
98 N — the crate's weight
About 33 N — the mass divided by μ

quizzes.q: A box rests on a 30° incline. What normal force does the surface exert?
o: N = mg cos 30° — only the component pressing into the slope
N = mg sin 30° — the component along the slope
N = mg — the surface always supports the full weight

quizzes.q: Spring A has k = 200 N/m and spring B has k = 800 N/m. The SAME 20 N force is applied to each. Which stretches further?
o: Spring B — a bigger k means a bigger extension
Both the same — the applied force is identical
Spring A — x = F/k, so 20/200 = 0.10 m versus 20/800 = 0.025 m

quizzes.q: How much elastic potential energy is stored in a spring of stiffness 400 N/m when it is extended by 0.10 m?
o: 40 J — force multiplied by extension, without the factor of a half
4.0 J — leaving out the half

quizzes.q: A car accelerates uniformly from rest at 2 m/s² for 5 s. How far does it travel, and what is its final speed?
o: 10 m, reaching 25 m/s
50 m, reaching 10 m/s
25 m, reaching 10 m/s

quizzes.q: What is the condition under which the SUVAT kinematic equations work?
o: They work for any motion, constant acceleration or not
Constant (uniform) acceleration

quizzes.q: A passenger standing in a bus lurches forward when the driver brakes sharply. How does the First Law account for this?
o: The passenger’s inertia acts as a force pushing them forward
The bus slows, but the passenger keeps moving at the old velocity until something acts on them — no forward force is needed
The brakes transfer their force through the floor into the passenger
Braking produces a forward force that throws the passenger down the bus

quizzes.q: The First Law covers two states as equally "unchanged". Which two?
o: At rest, and slowing down steadily
Moving forwards, and moving backwards
At rest, and moving at constant velocity in a straight line

quizzes.q: A resultant force of 24 N acts on a 6 kg mass. What acceleration does it produce?
o: 144 m/s²
4 m/s²
18 m/s²

quizzes.q: In F = ma, which quantity is "m": 60 kg or 600 N?
o: 600 N — since it’s the bigger number it must be the mass
60 kg — mass; 600 N would be weight

quizzes.q: A book rests on a table. The Earth pulls the book down. Which force is that pull’s Third-Law PARTNER?
o: The weight of the book acting downwards
The book’s downward push on the table
The table’s upward push on the book
The book’s gravitational pull upwards on the Earth

quizzes.q: If every force has an equal and opposite partner, why does anything ever accelerate instead of everything cancelling?
o: The partner force is slightly smaller, leaving a surplus
They do cancel, and motion comes from a separate non-paired force
The two forces act on DIFFERENT objects, and cancellation only happens between forces on the same body

quizzes.q: A 5 kg book sits on a flat table. What is the normal force? Now put it on a 30° incline — what is N now? (g = 10)
o: Both 50 N — the normal force is always equal to the weight
Flat: N = 50 N; incline: N = mg cos30° ≈ 43.3 N (less than weight)

quizzes.q: A 10 kg box sits on a level floor. A rope pulls it with a tension of 40 N at 30° ABOVE the horizontal, and the box stays in contact with the floor. What is the normal force from the floor? (g = 9.8 m/s², sin 30° = 0.5)
o: 58 N — the whole 40 N tension is subtracted from the weight
118 N — the rope adds 20 N to the weight
98 N — the normal force equals the weight
78 N — the rope's upward part (40 × sin 30° = 20 N) carries some of the 98 N weight

quizzes.q: A 5 kg block rests on a smooth 30° incline. A horizontal push of 10 N is applied to the block. What is the normal force acting on the block?
o: ≈ 42 N (just mg cos θ)
≈ 47 N (includes the push’s perpendicular component)
≈ 49 N (equal to the weight)
≈ 55 N (larger than the weight plus push)

quizzes.q: A block of mass m rests stationary on a frictionless incline at angle θ to the horizontal. What is the normal force N?
o: N = mg cosθ — resolved perpendicular to the slope
N = mg — the normal force always equals the weight

quizzes.q: A submerged hollow ball has a small hole drilled in its side. From which direction does water enter?
o: From whichever direction the hole faces — fluid pressure acts in all directions at a given point
Only from directly above, since fluid pressure acts downward

quizzes.q: What is the pressure due to the water alone at a depth of 3.0 m in a freshwater lake? (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s²)
o: 3000 Pa — density multiplied by depth, without g
9800 Pa — the pressure at 1 m, for any depth
About 29 kPa

quizzes.q: A 5 kg lamp hangs at rest from a single vertical cord. What is the tension in the cord? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
o: 0 N — nothing is moving, so there is no force
49 N — it must balance the lamp’s weight
98 N — twice the weight, one for each end of the cord
5 N — the tension equals the mass

quizzes.q: Two masses hang on either side of a pulley — 3 kg on the left, 5 kg on the right. The system accelerates. Is the tension equal to 5g (the heavier mass’s weight)?
o: Yes — tension always equals the weight of the heavier hanging mass
No — if T = 5g, the 5 kg mass would have zero net force and couldn’t accelerate; T is between 3g and 5g

quizzes.q: A drone flies 40 m due east in 8 s. State its average velocity.
o: 0.2 m/s due east
5 m/s due east
5 m/s

quizzes.q: Speed and velocity are defined with the same denominator. What exactly differs?
o: The numerator: speed uses distance (every metre travelled), velocity uses displacement (the straight arrow from start to finish)
The denominator: velocity divides by a shorter time
Nothing formally — "velocity" is the technical word for the same quantity

quizzes.q: A 300 K block touches a 280 K block. In which direction does heat spontaneously flow?
o: From the 300 K block to the 280 K block (high T to low T)
From the 280 K block to the 300 K block, to equalize faster

quizzes.q: Speed can be measured in metres per second, or in kilometres per hour. Are those two the same kind of quantity, or different kinds? Why?
o: Same kind — both are length over time, i.e. the same dimension [L][T]⁻¹
Different — different units means different dimensions

quizzes.q: Do m/s and km/h have the same dimension? Is ½ (as in ½mv²) dimensionless?
o: Yes to both — m/s and km/h are both [L][T]⁻¹; ½ is a pure number, dimensionless
No — different units always mean different dimensions, and ½ carries units of its own

quizzes.q: Three students measure the same rod and each gets 12.41 cm, every time, very consistently — but the ruler's zero mark is worn away and starts at 2 mm. Is 12.41 cm the true length? Why?
o: Yes — they all agree with each other, so the measurement must be right
No — the worn zero shifts every reading the same way; the result is consistent but wrong (precise but not accurate)

quizzes.q: A stopwatch always starts 0.3 s late — is that a systematic or random error? Scatter from pressing a timer at slightly different moments — systematic or random?
o: Both are random, since they both involve timing
Systematic (consistent 0.3 s late); random (scatter from timing variation)

quizzes.q: A car travels at 60 km/h. Is that a scalar or a vector?
o: Scalar — speed has no direction; velocity would be the vector
Vector — because speed has a direction

quizzes.q: You multiply 3.2 (two significant figures) by 4.56 (three significant figures). What is the correctly rounded result?
You multiply 2.5 (two significant figures) by 3.42 (three). To how many significant figures should the result be quoted?
o: Three
However many the calculator displays
Two — a product carries the precision of its LEAST precise input
Five — two plus three

quizzes.q: Both sides of a rectangle are measured to 2 significant figures each. To how many significant figures should the calculated area (their product) be reported?
o: 2 significant figures — a calculated result can never be more precise than its least precise input; multiplication/division keeps the fewest sig figs among the inputs
As many significant figures as the calculator displays for the product, since the calculation itself is exact

quizzes.q: Convert 72 km/h into metres per second.
o: 20 m/s
259 m/s — multiplying by 3.6 instead of dividing
1.2 m/s — dividing by 60 only, as though the hour were a minute

quizzes.q: Which of the following is an SI base unit?
o: litre
metre
hour
gram

quizzes.q: A box is pulled with a 3 N force pointing east and a 4 N force pointing north, at the same time. What single force do they add up to?
o: 5 N, north-east — using the right-angle triangle rule, √(3²+4²)
7 N — simply add the magnitudes together

quizzes.q: A box is pulled with a 3 N force pointing east and a 4 N force pointing north, at the same time. What is the magnitude of the single resultant force?
o: 7 N — simply add the two magnitudes together, 3 N + 4 N
5 N — found via the Pythagorean theorem √(3²+4²), since the two forces are perpendicular and add head-to-tail, not by simply adding the magnitudes

quizzes.q: A train speeds up from 12 m/s to 30 m/s in 6 seconds. What is its average acceleration?
o: 5 m/s²
3 m/s²
18 m/s²

quizzes.q: A 0.1 m × 0.1 m block is submerged with top at depth 3 m and bottom at 3.1 m in water. What is the net upward force from pressure alone?
o: 0 N — pressure at both faces is the same
9.8 N net upward (bottom pressure force exceeds top pressure force)

quizzes.q: A 1 kg steel ball sinks in water; a 1000 kg steel ship floats. What determines whether an object floats or sinks?
o: Average density compared to the fluid’s density — not weight
Weight — heavier objects sink, lighter objects float

quizzes.q: You walk 3 m forward and then 3 m back to where you started. What is the distance you covered? What is the displacement?
o: Distance = 6 m; displacement = 0 m
Both distance and displacement = 6 m

quizzes.q: A box on a frictionless floor is pulled by two forces at once: 20 N due east and 8 N due north. What is the resultant force?
o: 12 N due east — subtract the smaller from the larger
160 N — multiply them
About 21.5 N, pointing between east and north
28 N — add the two sizes together

quizzes.q: A ball has left a thrower's hand and is still rising through the air (ignore air resistance). Which forces belong on the ball's free-body diagram?
o: Only its weight, pointing down — the hand's push ended the moment the ball left it
Its weight, plus an upward force stored from the throw that runs out as the ball slows
Its weight pointing down, and the force of the throw pointing up and carrying the ball

quizzes.q: A lamp hangs at rest from the ceiling by a single cord. How many forces act on the lamp, and what are they?
o: Two — its weight down and the cord's tension up
One — only the tension in the cord
None — it is not moving
Three — weight, tension, and the ceiling pulling on the lamp

quizzes.q: A 10 kg box sits on a rough floor (μ_s = 0.4). You push it horizontally with 20 N and it does NOT move. What is the friction force on it right now? (g = 10)
o: 20 N — static friction matches the push to keep it still (below the 40 N maximum)
40 N — friction always equals μ_s × N

quizzes.q: A block slides across a table. If it were sliding twice as fast (at everyday speeds), what would happen to the kinetic friction on it?
o: About the same — kinetic friction is roughly μk × N, whatever the speed
It would double — faster sliding means more friction
It would disappear — friction only acts on slow objects

quizzes.q: A spring hangs from a ceiling with a 0.5 kg mass attached, in equilibrium. What is the spring force, and its direction?
o: F_spring = mg = 4.9 N downward
F_spring = mg = 4.9 N upward (balances weight)

quizzes.q: A spring calibrated as F = kx for small extensions is stretched far past its elastic limit. Does F = kx (with the original k) still correctly predict the force?
o: No — beyond the elastic limit the spring deforms permanently and the linear F = kx model no longer applies
Yes — Hooke’s Law applies to any extension of any spring

quizzes.q: You know the initial velocity, the acceleration and the TIME, and you want the final velocity. Which constant-acceleration equation gives it in one step?
o: s = ½(u + v)t
v² = u² + 2as
s = ut + ½at²
v = u + at

quizzes.q: What is the sign of the car’s acceleration?
o: Positive
Negative

quizzes.q: A silicon sample is heated from 20°C to 100°C. What happens to its resistivity?
o: It increases, following the same positive-temperature-coefficient formula R = R₀[1+αΔT] used for metals
It decreases dramatically (over 100-fold) — heating excites many more electrons across the band gap into the conduction band, exponentially increasing carrier density

quizzes.q: What is the difference between resistance and resistivity?
o: They are the same quantity expressed in different units
Resistivity depends on how much current is flowing; resistance does not
Resistance is the material property and resistivity depends on the shape
Resistance depends on the object's length and cross-section; resistivity is a property of the MATERIAL alone, independent of shape

quizzes.q: A wire of resistance R is stretched uniformly to twice its original length, with no metal lost. What is its new resistance?
o: 2R — the length has doubled
R — stretching does not change the material
4R

quizzes.q: Inductor A has L = 1 H carrying I = 0.1 A. Inductor B has L = 0.01 H (100 times smaller) carrying I = 10 A (100 times larger). Which one stores more energy?
o: Inductor B — U = ½LI² depends on current SQUARED, so B's much larger current more than compensates for its smaller inductance, giving it 100 times more stored energy
Inductor A — since it has the larger inductance L, and larger L always means more energy stored

quizzes.q: In an RL circuit connected to a battery, a very long time has passed and the current has reached a completely steady value. What is the back-EMF of the inductor at this point, and how much opposition does it present?
o: Back-EMF = 0 (since dI/dt = 0), and the inductor behaves like a plain wire, presenting zero opposition to the steady current
The back-EMF stays at its initial value, since inductors permanently oppose and reduce current flow

quizzes.q: A steady current flows through an inductor and the switch is suddenly OPENED. What does the inductor do?
o: It blocks the current more firmly than ever, since an inductor opposes current flow
It drives a large EMF trying to KEEP the current flowing, often arcing across the opening contacts. An inductor opposes CHANGE in current, so it can push current just as readily as resist it

quizzes.q: How much energy is stored in the magnetic field of a 0.50 H inductor carrying a steady current of 4.0 A?
o: 8.0 J — leaving out the factor of a half
2.0 J — using LI rather than LI²

quizzes.q: The field inside a long solenoid is B = μ₀nI. What does n stand for?
o: The total number of turns on the solenoid
The number of turns per unit area of the cross-section
The number of layers the coil is wound in
The number of turns per unit LENGTH of the solenoid

quizzes.q: Two solenoids have the same turns-per-length n and carry the same current I, but Solenoid A has radius 2 cm and Solenoid B has radius 20 cm (10 times wider). How do their internal field strengths compare?
o: They are exactly equal — B = μ₀nI has no radius dependence at all, so a wider solenoid gives the identical field strength inside as a narrower one with the same n and I
Solenoid B (wider) has a much stronger field, since it has more overall volume and coil material

quizzes.q: An MRI machine uses a very strong, real (finite) solenoid electromagnet. Is it accurate to say the field is exactly zero everywhere outside the solenoid, so no shielding is needed?
o: No — B = 0 outside is exact only for an idealized infinite solenoid; real, finite solenoids have genuine fringe fields near their ends that decay gradually (roughly 1/r³), which is exactly why MRI machines need substantial shielding
Yes — B = μ₀nI inside and B = 0 outside are both exact laws that apply to any real solenoid, so no external shielding should ever be necessary

quizzes.q: What is the magnetic flux density inside a long air-cored solenoid wound with 500 turns per metre and carrying 2.0 A? (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹)
o: About 1.3 × 10⁻³ T
About 1.3 T
About 1.3 × 10⁻⁶ T
About 6.3 × 10⁻⁴ T — leaving the current out

quizzes.q: A Wheatstone bridge is balanced and its galvanometer reads zero. What does that tell you?
o: The two mid-points of the bridge are at the same potential, so the resistance ratio in one arm equals the ratio in the other
All four resistances are equal to one another
The supply has failed or become disconnected
No current is flowing anywhere in the bridge

quizzes.q: A Wheatstone bridge is balanced (galvanometer reads zero), giving an unknown resistance X. The battery's EMF is then doubled. What happens to the measured value of X?
o: X stays exactly the same — the balance condition X = QR/P doesn't involve EMF at all, since balance is purely a ratio between the four resistors
X changes, since a larger EMF drives more current through the bridge and shifts the balance point

quizzes.q: A Wheatstone bridge has P = 100 Ω, Q = 10 Ω, R = 47 Ω, X = 4.7 Ω — four different resistor values. Can this bridge still be balanced (galvanometer reads zero)?
o: No — a Wheatstone bridge can only balance when all four resistors are equal to each other (P = Q = R = X)
Yes — balance only requires P/Q = R/X (here both equal 10), a ratio match; the four resistors do not need to be equal to each other

quizzes.q: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge, the galvanometer current is:
o: Zero
Maximum

quizzes.q: In a discovery announcement, is "invariant mass" the mass of one single particle the detector measured directly?
o: Yes — invariant mass is simply the measured mass of the particle that hit the detector
No — it is computed from the energies and momenta of two or more decay products via the relativistic energy-momentum relation, reconstructing the mass of a parent particle the detector never saw

quizzes.q: Why do particle physicists keep building accelerators of ever higher energy?
o: To push the particles past the speed of light
Creating a heavy particle needs at least its rest energy, by E = mc², and higher energy also resolves shorter distances
To heat the target hot enough to break its atoms apart
Because low-energy beams cannot be steered by magnets

quizzes.q: If a collider reaches an energy above the threshold needed to produce a certain particle, is that particle guaranteed to appear in every collision from that point forward?
o: No — meeting the energy threshold is necessary but not sufficient; production also has its own probability (cross-section), so many collisions are still needed to actually produce and detect the particle
Yes — once you have enough energy, the particle should just show up reliably in every subsequent collision

quizzes.q: A charged particle leaves a curved track in a detector sitting in a magnetic field. What does the curvature tell you?
o: The ratio of its momentum to its charge — and the DIRECTION of the curve gives the sign of that charge
Its speed, and nothing else
Its lifetime before decaying
Its mass, read off directly

quizzes.q: Is the proton the antiparticle of the electron, since they have opposite charge?
o: No — a true antiparticle pair must match exactly in mass with only charge (and other quantum numbers) reversed; the proton is about 1836 times heavier than the electron, so it fails the mass-matching test
Yes — opposite electric charge is the defining property of an antiparticle pair, and the proton and electron have opposite charge

quizzes.q: An electron and a positron annihilate at rest. Is anything left afterwards?
o: No — "annihilate" means they cancel out to nothing and the energy is destroyed
Yes — two 511 keV photons carrying exactly the original rest-mass energy; this is precisely what a PET scanner detects, so if energy vanished PET imaging could not work

quizzes.q: How does an antiparticle differ from its corresponding particle?
o: Same mass and same spin, but opposite sign of electric charge and of the other additive quantum numbers
It travels backwards in time and therefore cannot be detected
It has the opposite mass — negative rather than positive
It is an ordinary particle that happens to carry negative energy

quizzes.q: Why is the matter–antimatter asymmetry of the universe regarded as an unsolved problem?
o: Because the existence of antimatter would violate conservation of energy
Because antimatter has never actually been observed
Because the Standard Model forbids antimatter outright

Known physics makes matter and antimatter in very nearly equal amounts. An almost-equal early universe should have annihilated into radiation, leaving no matter at all — so the small surviving imbalance is unexplained

quizzes.q: After decades of searching in detectors like Super-Kamiokande, has proton decay actually been observed?
o: No — none has been seen, which places the proton lifetime beyond 10^34 years if it decays at all; that null result is itself strong positive evidence for baryon number conservation
Yes — with that much searching over that many years, it must have been found by now

quizzes.q: A proposed reaction conserves energy and momentum perfectly, and plenty of energy is available. Is that enough to guarantee it can happen?
o: Yes — as long as there is enough energy and momentum is conserved, the reaction should be possible
No — baryon number and lepton number must also be conserved, as independent requirements separate from energy and momentum; violating either forbids the reaction regardless of available energy

quizzes.q: Besides energy, momentum and electric charge, which quantities must also be conserved in Standard-Model particle reactions?
o: Total mass and total volume
Colour charge, and nothing further
The magnitude of the spin, and nothing further
Baryon number, and each lepton flavour number separately

quizzes.q: Free neutron decay is written n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ. Check the baryon and lepton numbers on each side.
o: Baryon number is not conserved, since a proton is not a neutron
Lepton number is not conserved, because an electron appears where there was none
Baryon number 1 → 1, and lepton number 0 → (+1) + (−1) = 0. Both are conserved
Neither is conserved, which is why the decay needs the weak force

quizzes.q: If electromagnetism and the weak force are unified, why do they look so different in every ordinary lab experiment?
o: They should not look different — if they were truly unified they would behave identically at any energy
Because unification is an energy-dependent claim — the two become indistinguishable only above about 100 GeV; below that, electroweak symmetry breaking makes them genuinely, measurably different

quizzes.q: If electromagnetism and the weak force are really one force, why do they look nothing alike in ordinary experiments?
o: They are not genuinely unified — "electroweak" is just a convenient label
They only look different because the weak force is harder to measure accurately
The symmetry is BROKEN at low energy: the W and Z are very heavy, so the weak force is short-ranged and feeble, while the massless photon is not. At very high energy the two behave alike
Because electromagnetism acts on charge and the weak force does not act on charged particles at all

quizzes.q: Has electroweak unification already merged all four fundamental forces — gravity, electromagnetism, the strong force, and the weak force — into one single theory?
o: No — electroweak unification merges only electromagnetism and the weak force; Grand Unification (adding the strong force) is unconfirmed and quantum gravity remains unsolved
Yes — "unification" means all the forces are now understood as one single theory

quizzes.q: Did electroweak theory make any specific, falsifiable numerical prediction that could have proven it wrong, or is it just a way of writing the math more elegantly?
o: No — electroweak unification is just a more elegant way to write already-known equations, with no genuinely new, testable prediction attached
Yes — it predicted the W and Z boson masses (via the weak mixing angle) in the 1960s, decades before technology existed to test it, confirmed by direct discovery at CERN in 1983

quizzes.q: Which statement about the lines in a Feynman diagram is correct?
o: The lines show the exact trajectories particles follow in space
The lines indicate which particles interact and the exchanged force carrier, not actual paths
The lines represent the speed of each particle
The lines are purely decorative and have no physical meaning

quizzes.q: Feynman diagrams draw antiparticle lines with the arrow pointing backward in time. Have antiparticles been observed travelling backward through time?
o: No — every antiparticle ever detected moves forward through time like everything else; the backward arrow is a bookkeeping convention reflecting a mathematical equivalence in the field-theory terms
Yes — antiparticles really do travel backward in time, and the diagrams record that observation

quizzes.q: Why do Feynman diagrams with more vertices usually contribute less to the final result?
o: Because they describe processes that cannot physically happen
Every vertex brings another factor of the coupling constant, which in QED is about 1/137 — so each extra vertex shrinks the contribution
Because they violate conservation laws
Because they are more difficult to draw correctly

quizzes.q: Rank the four fundamental forces by relative strength, strongest first.
o: They are all of broadly comparable strength
Gravitational, electromagnetic, weak, strong
Electromagnetic, strong, gravitational, weak
Strong, electromagnetic, weak, gravitational

quizzes.q: List the four fundamental forces. Is friction one of them?
o: Yes — friction is a force you can draw an arrow for and use in F=ma, so it belongs alongside gravity, electromagnetism, strong, and weak as a fifth fundamental force

No — friction is a macroscopic electromagnetic effect (electron-cloud repulsion between touching surfaces) with no independent coupling constant; the four fundamental forces are gravity, electromagnetism, strong, and weak

quizzes.q: Which force holds the Solar System together — the strong force or gravity? Why doesn't the strong force do it, if it's the strongest of the four?
o: The strong force — since it is the strongest of the four fundamental forces, it should dominate at every scale, including planetary distances
Gravity — the strong force's range is cut off completely beyond about 10⁻¹⁵ m, so at planetary separations its effect is exactly zero, not just weak

quizzes.q: Both gravity and the weak nuclear force get called "weak". Is the weak nuclear force just gravity at a smaller scale?
o: Yes — they are the same kind of long-range attraction, the weak force simply being the smaller of the two

No — gravity has infinite range and never changes what a particle IS; the weak force has a range of about 10^-18 m and is the only force that converts one quark or lepton into another, as in beta decay

quizzes.q: Has the graviton actually been detected, the same way the photon, gluon, and W/Z bosons have been?
o: Yes — since each of the four fundamental forces has a mediating gauge boson, and the other three are confirmed, the graviton must already be confirmed too
No — the graviton remains a purely theoretical, never-directly-detected proposal, unlike the experimentally confirmed photon, gluon, and W/Z bosons

quizzes.q: Is a photon a building block of matter, the same way a quark or an electron is?
o: Yes — photons, gluons and W/Z bosons are simply more entries on the same particle list
No — quarks and leptons are fermions and are what matter is built from; gauge bosons are the force carriers, appearing transiently as an interaction is transmitted rather than composing bulk matter

quizzes.q: Which carrier goes with which force — electromagnetism, the strong force, the weak force, in that order?
o: Photon, the W and Z bosons, and gluon
Photon, gluon, and the W and Z bosons
Gluon, photon, and the W and Z bosons
Graviton, gluon, and photon

quizzes.q: The W and Z bosons are far heavier than the photon. Does that mean the weak force should have a longer range than electromagnetism?
o: No — the relationship is inverted via the uncertainty principle: heavier mediators produce SHORTER-range forces, which is exactly why the weak force is extremely short-range while electromagnetism is infinite-range
Yes — a heavier mediating particle should carry force further, the same way a heavier object travels further with momentum

quizzes.q: If three quarks make a baryon, do two quarks alone (no antiquark) make an ordinary hadron?
o: Yes — quarks combine to form hadrons, so any number of them should give some valid hadron

No — colour neutrality is the constraint, and it is satisfied by three quarks (one of each colour) or a quark-antiquark pair, not by two quarks; tetraquarks and pentaquarks exist but are rare, recently-confirmed exotics

quizzes.q: A proton has charge +1 and baryon number +1. Does that mean charge and baryon number are always the same number for any hadron?
o: No — they are computed by independent rules; the neutron has charge 0 but baryon number +1, showing the two quantities plainly diverge
Yes — since they match for the proton, baryon number and electric charge must be the same underlying quantity under different names

quizzes.q: The proton's mass is about 938 MeV/c². Its three quarks have masses of roughly 2, 2, and 5 MeV/c². Do these numbers add up?
o: No — the quark masses sum to barely 1% of the proton's mass; the overwhelming remainder comes from strong-force binding energy, not the bare quark masses
Yes — a hadron's mass should simply be the sum of its constituent quark masses, the same way a composite object's mass sums its parts

quizzes.q: What quark content makes a baryon, and what makes a meson?
o: A baryon is a quark and an antiquark; a meson is three quarks
Both are three quarks, differing only in mass
A baryon is three quarks; a meson is one quark and one antiquark
A baryon is two quarks; a meson is three

quizzes.q: Is the Higgs boson (discovered in 2012) the same thing as the Higgs field, or are they related but different?
o: They are the same thing — "the Higgs boson" and "the Higgs field" are just two names for one identical entity
Related but different — the field is the pervasive, space-filling mechanism (present even in vacuum); the boson is a distinct, detectable particle-like excitation of that field

quizzes.q: Does the Higgs mechanism explain why the photon is massless, or does it give mass to the photon too?
o: It explains why the photon stays massless — the photon has exactly zero coupling to the Higgs field, a consequence of the underlying gauge symmetries
The Higgs field gives mass to everything, including the photon, since it is described as "the particle that gives everything mass"

quizzes.q: Almost all the mass of an everyday object does NOT come from the Higgs field. Where does it come from?
o: From the Higgs field — essentially all of it
From the electrons in the atoms
From the weak nuclear force
The binding energy of the gluon field inside protons and neutrons. The quarks' own Higgs-given masses account for only a small percentage of a nucleon's mass

quizzes.q: Was 2012 when physicists first proposed the Higgs mechanism?
o: No — the mechanism was proposed in 1964 and its framework was already confirmed indirectly by the 1983 W and Z discovery; 2012 confirmed the Higgs BOSON, the last missing piece of a 48-year story
Yes — the Higgs mechanism was discovered in 2012

quizzes.q: Are muons and tau particles floating around in the atoms of this room right now, the same way electrons are?
o: No — only the electron is stable and common at everyday conditions; muons and tau particles decay away in microseconds or less and must be freshly produced to exist at all
Yes — since there are six leptons total, all six should be present in roughly equal amounts in ordinary matter

quizzes.q: Is the muon less fundamental than the electron, because it is heavy and unstable?
o: Yes — the electron is a real fundamental particle, while the muon is an exotic heavy cousin that decays away
No — the muon has the same charge, the same spin and no more internal structure than the electron; it is simply heavier, so it decays. Fundamental does not mean stable

quizzes.q: When a muon decays, does it just lose some mass and turn into an electron, or does something else happen?
o: Yes — the muon simply loses weight and becomes an electron, since "the muon decays into an electron" describes the whole process
Something else — it is a genuine three-particle event: muon → electron + muon-neutrino + electron-antineutrino, not a simple mass-loss transformation

quizzes.q: How many CHARGED leptons are there, and what are they?
o: Six charged leptons, matching the six quarks
Two — the electron and the muon
One — the electron; the others are composite
Three — the electron, the muon and the tau, each paired with its own neutrino

quizzes.q: Which statement about neutrino mass is correct?
o: Neutrinos are exactly massless
Neutrinos have a small but nonzero mass
Neutrinos have the same mass as electrons
Neutrinos have variable mass depending on flavor

quizzes.q: Neutrino oscillation — a neutrino changing flavour in flight — was a major discovery. What does it establish?
o: That neutrinos travel faster than light
That there are more than three neutrino flavours
That neutrinos have non-zero mass, which the original Standard Model did not permit
That neutrinos are their own antiparticles

quizzes.q: If neutrinos almost never interact with matter, how was the neutrino ever actually detected in an experiment?
o: Neutrinos never interact with matter at all, so they cannot actually be directly detected — their existence is inferred only indirectly
The interaction probability is extraordinarily small but genuinely nonzero; huge, carefully instrumented detectors (tens of thousands of tons of material) catch the rare interactions that do occur

quizzes.q: A neutron beta-decays. Which neutrino flavour comes out, and does the flavour label mean anything physical?
o: An electron-antineutrino specifically — never a muon or tau one. Flavour is conserved at the interaction vertex, which is exactly why solar electron-neutrino detectors measured a deficit once oscillation was in play
Any of the three — "flavour" is just a naming convention with no physical content

quizzes.q: What distinguishes a hadron from a lepton?
o: Hadrons are heavy and leptons are light, by definition
Hadrons are fermions and leptons are bosons
A hadron is built from quarks and feels the strong force; a lepton is fundamental and does not feel it
Hadrons are electrically charged and leptons are neutral

quizzes.q: Are protons and neutrons fundamental particles, in the particle-physics sense of having no internal structure?
o: Yes — protons, neutrons and electrons are the three basic building blocks and cannot be broken down further

No — deep inelastic scattering in the late 1960s found point-like constituents (quarks) inside the proton, exactly as Rutherford had found structure inside the atom; only the quarks and the electron are fundamental here

quizzes.q: Is a pion a baryon? Is it a hadron?
o: It is a hadron but NOT a baryon — the pion is a meson (a quark-antiquark pair); baryons are only one hadron sub-category (three-quark combinations like the proton and neutron)
Hadron and baryon mean the same thing, so if the pion is a hadron it must also be a baryon

quizzes.q: The tau lepton is heavier than the proton. Does that mean the tau is actually a hadron?
o: No — mass plays no role in hadron/lepton classification; the tau has no internal quark structure and does not feel the strong force, so it remains a lepton regardless of its mass
Yes — since the tau is heavier than the proton, and heavier particles are hadrons, the tau should be reclassified as a hadron

quizzes.q: Is there a strange quark or a top quark inside the atoms in this table right now?
o: No — only up and down quarks are stable and common at everyday energy scales; strange, top, charm, and bottom quarks require high-energy production and decay away almost instantly
Yes — since matter is made of quarks and there are six flavors, all six should be present in roughly equal amounts in ordinary matter

quizzes.q: Could a sensitive enough detector measure a lone charge of exactly +2/3 e sitting by itself?
o: No — confinement means quarks exist only inside hadrons, whose total charge is always a whole multiple of e; every charge ever measured directly has been a whole multiple of e
Yes — fractional charge is real, so a precise enough instrument should eventually read exactly +2/3 e on its own

quizzes.q: If you had an arbitrarily powerful particle accelerator, could you eventually pull a single quark out of a proton and study it alone?
o: Yes — with enough energy, any bound system can eventually be separated into its individual parts, the same way enough energy separates atoms or molecules

No — confinement means the binding force between quarks grows with separation; pulling them apart far enough creates a new quark-antiquark pair from the vacuum instead of ever releasing one free quark

quizzes.q: How many quark flavours are there, and what electric charges do they carry?
o: Six, all carrying a charge of ±1
Three, all carrying +1/3
Four, matching the four fundamental forces
Six — up, charm and top at +2/3, and down, strange and bottom at −1/3

quizzes.q: The Standard Model predicts the electron magnetic moment to extraordinary precision. Does that mean it is essentially complete?
o: No — precision within a domain and completeness beyond it are independent. Neutrino masses already required going past the original formulation, and dark matter, dark energy and gravity remain entirely unaddressed
Yes — a theory tested to that many decimal places cannot have major unresolved gaps left

quizzes.q: Are dark matter and dark energy the same kind of mystery — both just a matter of finding the right undiscovered particle?
o: No — dark matter is more likely a new, undiscovered particle actively searched for in detectors; dark energy is more often treated as a property of space itself (a cosmological constant), a fundamentally different kind of question
Yes — dark matter and dark energy are basically the same thing, just particles that have not yet been found

quizzes.q: The Standard Model arranges its matter particles into three GENERATIONS. What distinguishes them?
o: Each generation carries a different set of electric charges
The generations are ordered by the date on which they were discovered
Later generations contain more particles than earlier ones
Each generation repeats the same pattern of charges with progressively larger masses. Only the first is stable, and why there are exactly three is unexplained

quizzes.q: Does the Standard Model explain gravity? Does it explain dark matter and dark energy, which make up most of the universe's total mass-energy content?
o: No — the Standard Model explicitly excludes gravity entirely and has no explanation for dark matter or dark energy, which together make up about 95% of the universe's total mass-energy content
Yes — the Standard Model is a complete theory of everything, precisely tested and fully explaining all known physics

quizzes.q: Which of the following best describes what happens when two quarks are pulled farther apart?
o: The force weakens with distance, like gravity or electromagnetism.
The force grows stronger, making separation increasingly difficult.
The force becomes repulsive, pushing the quarks apart.
The force disappears altogether.

quizzes.q: As two quarks are pulled further apart, does the force between them get weaker, like it would for two charged particles or two masses?
o: Yes — all fundamental forces should weaken with distance the same way gravity and electromagnetism do
No — the strong force stays roughly constant or even grows with distance, like a stretching elastic band, the opposite of the 1/r² weakening pattern of gravity and electromagnetism

quizzes.q: What does ASYMPTOTIC FREEDOM mean for the strong interaction?
o: The strong force becomes infinitely large at very short range
The coupling gets WEAKER at short distance and high energy, so quarks move almost freely inside a hadron — the opposite of how electromagnetism behaves
Quarks become free once they are pulled far enough apart
Quarks escape their hadron at low energy

quizzes.q: If you could somehow look at a single quark, would it actually appear red, green or blue?
o: No — "colour charge" is a name, not a description; quarks are far smaller than any visible wavelength, and the word was borrowed only because three charges combining to neutral mirrors red+green+blue light making white
Yes — quarks are literally coloured, which is why it is called colour charge

quizzes.q: If the weak interaction stopped working tomorrow, would much change?
o: Enormously — the Sun's proton-proton chain needs a weak step to turn a proton into a neutron, so every main-sequence star would go dark; all beta decay would stop too. "Weak" describes coupling strength, not importance
Almost nothing — the weak force is weak, so it does not really do much

quizzes.q: If you built a mirror-image version of a radioactive decay experiment, would the results look exactly the same, just flipped?
o: Yes — physics should look the same in a mirror, and that symmetry holds for every fundamental force including the weak interaction

No — the weak interaction violates parity (the 1956 Wu experiment showed beta decay emits electrons preferentially in one direction relative to nuclear spin), unlike gravity, EM, and the strong force which all conserve parity

quizzes.q: What is beta-minus decay at the QUARK level?
o: An electron is ejected from the atom's electron shell
An up quark turns into a down quark, emitting a W⁺ boson
A neutron splits into a proton and an electron that were already inside it
A down quark turns into an up quark, emitting a W⁻ boson, which then decays into an electron and an electron antineutrino

quizzes.q: What can the weak interaction do that no other fundamental force can?
o: Act on electrically neutral particles
Hold the nucleus together against electrostatic repulsion
Change the FLAVOUR of a quark or a lepton — turning a down quark into an up quark, which is what makes beta decay possible
Act across an unlimited range
